text: The close has dropped from nine days to four.
In the second week the nightly sync failed for three days.
Nobody has typed an invoice by hand since July.
In 2024 the team closed the month in nine days.
They chose us in January and ran a pilot in one plant.
We had one bad week, and it has not happened again.
Since then the close has dropped from nine days to four.
Their finance director has agreed to take your call.

I have written about two hundred case studies, and most of the ones that failed made the same mistake. They started with the product. Nobody cares about the product in the first paragraph. They care about the customer, and they care about one number: where the customer was before anything changed. That is the baseline, and without it every result is just an adjective. Faster than what? Cheaper than when? So the order I use is always the same. First, the situation, in the past, with a date. Then what the customer decided, and what happened, also in the past. And only then the results, in the present, because the results are still true today. The close has dropped to four days. Adoption has reached ninety per cent. If the numbers are still true, say them as if they are still true. And one more thing. Put in the part that went wrong. Buyers do not believe stories where nothing went wrong.

When a vendor sends me a case study, I read it in about forty seconds, and I am looking for three things. The first is a name I can call. A logo on a slide is not a reference. A finance director who has agreed to take my call is a reference. The second is a baseline with a date on it, because an improvement of sixty per cent means nothing if I do not know what it was sixty per cent of. And the third is the problem. Every implementation I have ever seen has had a bad week, and when a case study has no bad week in it, I assume somebody has removed it. So the case studies that actually move me are the honest ones. Here is what went wrong, here is when it happened, here is how quickly it was fixed, and here is what has changed since. That last sentence is the one I remember.
In 2024 the team closed the month in nine days.
Since then the close has dropped from nine days to four.
They have used the platform for eighteen months.
We had one bad week, and it has not happened again.
Without a baseline, sixty per cent faster means nothing.
Invoice turnaround time has fallen from three days to one.
They chose us in January and ran a pilot in one plant.
Their finance director has agreed to take your call.
